title: Insurance coverage can become less complete before probable dementia onset while Medicaid eligibility rises without higher take-up
source_unit: NBER Working Paper 35606, retrospective Health and Retirement Study analysis of Medicare supplemental coverage around probable dementia onset
geography: United States; Medicare-enrolled Health and Retirement Study adults age 65 and older, 2000-2016

observations.period: Four years before through two years before probable dementia onset, with matched comparison adults

denominator.unit: 3,001 Medicare-enrolled adults with probable dementia and 14,055 matched controls in the Health and Retirement Study

medicare_without_supplemental_coverage.unit: percentage-point higher probability for people with probable dementia four years before onset than matched controls

coverage_composition.value: the difference reflected lower likelihood of Medicare Advantage or traditional Medicare with supplemental coverage and higher likelihood of Medicaid

medicaid_eligibility.unit: percentage-point higher Medicaid eligibility two years before onset

medicaid_takeup.value: take-up rates were comparable despite the eligibility difference

care_financial_outcome.value: not observed in the public abstract
care_financial_outcome.unit: missing out-of-pocket spending, care use, caregiver burden, coverage continuity, and later financial security

observations.method: Retrospective secondary-data analysis of the 2000-2016 Health and Retirement Study using propensity-score weights and matched controls; probable dementia is assessed with the Langa-Weir approach and interviewer assessments for proxy interviews.
observations.uncertainty: The abstract reports coverage changes around probable onset but does not disclose the full timing structure, reasons for coverage changes, plan generosity, premiums, claims, or care outcomes. Probable dementia is a study measure and is not the same as a clinical diagnosis for every respondent.
observations.subgroup: Medicare-enrolled adults age 65 and older with probable dementia and matched controls; the abstract does not provide a complete breakdown by race, wealth, living arrangement, caregiver access, rurality, or state Medicaid rules.
observations.counterinterpretation: Coverage differences may reflect changing income, assets, health needs, living arrangements, institutional transitions, or eligibility rules rather than dementia itself. Comparable Medicaid take-up does not show that enrollment assistance would work, and incomplete supplemental coverage does not by itself establish unaffordable or inadequate care.

boundary: This record measures Medicare supplemental-coverage and Medicaid-eligibility differences around probable dementia onset in a historical U.S. survey panel. It does not establish causation, actual care affordability or quality, caregiver burden, financial harm, or the effect of enrollment assistance.
